name_en: Li Zhi Hong Cha (Lychee Black Tea)
processing: Black tea flavoured with lychee. Methods differ by maker, from scenting with fruit to adding juice or flavouring, so there is no single recipe; ask what was used.
harvest_season: Not tied to one picking; the base is an ordinary black tea, and the flavouring is done afterwards.
appearance_dry: Dark, fine twisted leaf, as is typical of a Chinese black tea base.
taste_profile: A soft black tea with a sweet, floral lychee aroma; low astringency is typical of the better lots, while strong added flavouring can taste like perfume.

brewing.notes: Normally brewed Western-style. Over-steeping leaves the base tea bitter under the aroma; it is also good iced.

vintage_note: Sold without vintage as a flavoured everyday tea. The aroma is the point and it fades, so buy small amounts and drink them within about a year.
description:
This is black tea with lychee added, a flavoured style most often linked with Guangdong, where both lychees and black tea are grown. It is sold under its Chinese name in Russian-speaking shops too, and sometimes misspelled there.

There is no standard method. Some makers scent or blend with fruit and others use juice or flavouring, and labels are not always clear about which. That difference, more than anything else, decides the quality.

Expect a soft cup with a sweet floral fruit nose. Use water slightly off the boil and do not let it stand, since the base tea is what turns bitter. It works well cold.

Look at the ingredient list if there is one. A very loud aroma often means flavouring, which is not a sin as long as it is honest. Buy small, since the scent fades.
history: Little is documented about the origin of lychee black tea, and no reliable date or inventor is on record. Lychee-flavoured products are a current line of development in Guangdong: one company in Zhenlong, Huizhou, says it began developing a lychee black tea in 2014, and the Yingde black tea industry has also added it to its range.
